transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... honestly, ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, things have just been off. I mean, I'm holding it together at work—I'm an EMT, so I have to be on my game there. You can't exactly lose focus when you're in the back of an ambulance, you know? Just last week we had this call, a guy fell off his roof trying to clean his gutters. I always tell my wife, hire somebody for the gutters, it's not worth the copay. But anyway, at home and with my coursework, I'm just way more wound up and short-tempered than I'm used to being. It's like I have no patience left. And I've even started skipping the things that usually keep my head clear—fishing, woodworking, those first-aid workshops I usually help out with. I used to love making these little wooden birdhouses, actually. My grandfather taught me how to do it when I was a kid. He had this old shed out back... but yeah, I just haven't had the energy or the mindset for any of that lately.
Are you avoiding your father-in-law or social interactions in general since he moved in?

Well, I don't know if I'm avoiding him, exactly. It's more like... I just don't have the energy to be around anyone when I get home. But it's not like I'm hiding in my room or anything. I mean, my wife and I still watch TV in the living room. Although, lately, it's just been reruns of that old detective show she likes. You know the one with the guy who always wears the trench coat? I used to watch that with my dad all the time. He actually had a coat just like that, bought it at some army surplus store back in the eighties. Wore it everywhere until the lining fell out. But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, avoiding people. I guess I just haven't really noticed if I'm doing it on purpose. I just feel kind of drained, you know?
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time since your father-in-law moved in?

Sad or empty? Hmm. I wouldn't say sad, exactly. Empty? I don't know, maybe just... tapped out. Like I said, I'm just drained. But sad? No, I don't think so. I mean, my wife was sad the other day because they discontinued her favorite brand of coffee at the grocery store. It's this hazelnut blend she's been drinking since we got married. I tried telling her we could just buy the syrup and make it ourselves, but she says it's not the same. We actually met at a coffee shop, believe it or not. Back when I was doing my undergrad. She spilled a latte on my textbook. Good thing it was just an elective, Introduction to Sociology, I think. The professor was this guy with a massive beard who always talked about his cats. Anyway, yeah, I'm not really feeling sad or empty, just... tired and wound up.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things that are coming up or things that might happen in the future?

Worrying about the future? I don't really think so. I mean, I try not to get too far ahead of myself. You kind of learn to do that in my line of work, you know? You just deal with what's right in front of you. Like last month, we had to replace the transmission on the rig, and the fleet mechanic was swearing up and down that it would take three weeks to get the parts. He's this guy, Gary, always chewing on a toothpick. I don't know how he doesn't swallow it by accident. My uncle used to chew on toothpicks, actually, until he chipped a tooth on one. Cost him a fortune at the dentist. He was furious. But yeah, no, I don't really sit around worrying about what's coming up. I just try to get through the day right now.
Do you feel anxious most of the time?

Anxious most of the time? I mean... I wouldn't say *most* of the time. Just, you know, wound up lately with the house being so crowded. But anxious in general? Nah. It's funny you ask about being anxious, though, because my partner on the ambulance, Dave, he's the anxious one. Guy practically vibrates if we get a call anywhere near the interstate. He got rear-ended by a semi truck about five years ago—totaled his Honda Civic. He loved that car, had this custom paint job he did himself in his garage. Used a spray gun and everything. Took him three weekends. His wife was so mad because the whole house smelled like paint fumes. She ended up taking the kids to her sister's place in Ohio for a week just to get away from the smell. They have this really nice cabin out there near a lake, great fishing. I went up there once and caught a bass the size of my forearm. But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I don't think I feel anxious most of the time. Just... tense, I guess.
Do you often feel irritable?

Irritable? Yeah, I guess you could say that. I'm definitely more short than I'm used to. Like I said, I've been holding it together at work on the ambulance, but at home and with my coursework, I'm just so wound up since my father-in-law moved in. I'm taking these continuing education classes for my EMT recertification, mostly online. The interface on the website is terrible, though. It keeps logging me out if I'm inactive for like, two minutes. I called their tech support last week and the guy on the phone sounded like he was eating potato chips the whole time. Crunch, crunch, crunch right in my ear. It reminded me of this guy I used to fish with, Carl. He always brought these massive bags of salt and vinegar chips on the boat. We used to go out every weekend, actually. I've been skipping that lately, though. Skipping my woodworking projects in the garage, too, and those first-aid workshops I usually help run. They usually keep my head clear, you know? But Carl, he'd eat those chips and get the grease all over his fishing rod. Once he dropped his favorite reel right in the water because his hands were so slippery. We spent an hour trying to fish it out with a net. Never found it. But yeah, to answer your question, I'm definitely more irritable and short at home these days.
Are you avoiding certain activities or places because of your father-in-law's presence?

Avoiding places? No, I wouldn't say I'm avoiding things on purpose. I mean, I'm just... around less, I guess. It's not like I'm hiding from him. Though, you know, my garage used to be my sanctuary. I had this whole setup for my woodworking. Custom workbench I built myself out of reclaimed oak. Found the wood at this old barn they were tearing down out on Route 9. The guy who owned the land, old farmer named Henderson, said the barn had been there since the 1920s. He had this three-legged dog that followed him everywhere. Sweetest dog, a golden retriever mix, I think. Missing its front left leg, but it still ran faster than most dogs with all four. Henderson said it got caught in a tractor when it was a pup. Tractor accidents are nasty, man. We get calls for those sometimes on the ambulance, and it's never pretty. You really have to know your trauma protocols for those. But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right. No, I'm not avoiding activities because of him, I just haven't had the energy to get out to the garage or do much else lately.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite since your father-in-law moved in?

Appetite? Hmm, no, not really. I mean, I'm eating about the same. Maybe a little more junk food on shift, but that's normal for me. Speaking of junk food, you wouldn't believe the spread they had at the station yesterday. One of the new guys, a rookie named Tyler, his mom runs a bakery downtown. It's that little place on Main Street with the green awning, you know the one? Anyway, she sent him in with two massive boxes of pastries. Bear claws, eclairs, these little fruit tarts with kiwi and strawberries on top. The kiwi was perfectly ripe, too. You don't always get that. Usually, kiwi is either rock hard or complete mush. I tried growing kiwis once in my backyard, actually. Built this whole trellis system out of PVC pipe and some heavy-duty netting. Took me an entire weekend to put it together, and I had to dig the post holes by hand because my auger broke. Snapped the shear pin right in half on a huge rock. I ended up taking it to this small engine repair guy a few towns over. Older guy, had a shop that smelled like two-stroke oil and stale coffee. He fixed it in about five minutes and only charged me ten bucks. Honestly, you don't find honest mechanics like that much anymore. But, uh... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, my appetite. No, I haven't really noticed any change there. Just eating like normal, I guess.
Have you lost or gained a significant amount of weight since your father-in-law moved in?

Weight? No, I don't think so. My uniform pants still fit the same, anyway. It's funny you mention uniforms, though, because they just changed our supplier at work. Used to be we got these really sturdy, cotton-blend cargo pants from a place up in Boston. They had these reinforced knees that were great for when you're kneeling on the pavement during a call. But the new ones? They're this weird synthetic material. They feel like windbreaker pants, you know? Every time you walk down the hallway at the station, it's just *swish, swish, swish*. Drives me crazy. Reminds me of the snow pants my mom used to make me wear when I was a kid. We lived near this massive hill—well, it felt massive when I was eight—and all the neighborhood kids would go sledding there. I had this plastic toboggan that was neon green. I thought it was the fastest thing on the planet until my buddy Mike showed up with a runner sled. One of those old-school wooden ones with the metal blades? Man, that thing flew. He wiped out at the bottom once and nearly took out Mrs. Gable's mailbox. She was this older lady who grew the most incredible hydrangeas. Huge blue blooms, big as your head. She said the secret was putting coffee grounds in the soil. I tried that with my tomatoes last year, but I think I used too much because the soil got all acidic and the leaves turned yellow. It's tricky getting the pH balance right in a garden. You really have to test the soil. But, um... what did you ask me? Right, weight. Yeah, no, I haven't noticed any weight changes. Pants still fit fine.
Do you feel like you're experiencing a range of emotions like you used to, or has that changed lately?

Emotions? I don't know, I guess I feel pretty much the same range of things. I'm not really numb or anything like that. I still get annoyed, especially when dispatch gives us a call right at the end of shift. That happened on Tuesday, actually. We were literally backing the rig into the bay, ten minutes left on the clock, and the tones drop. Code 3 for a motor vehicle accident out on the interstate. Turns out it was just a fender bender, but traffic was backed up for miles. We sat there idling on the shoulder for forty-five minutes waiting for a tow truck. The tow guy, his name was Lenny, he had this massive flatbed. Said he just bought it at auction down in Florida and drove it all the way up here. Florida's crazy right now with the humidity. My sister went to Orlando last month and said it felt like walking through soup. She brought back these little alligator keychains for my kids. The kind where the mouth opens and closes if you squeeze the back? My youngest broke his in about three seconds. He's always taking things apart to see how they work. Reminds me of when I took apart my dad's lawnmower when I was ten. I thought I could make it run faster if I adjusted the carburetor, but I ended up stripping a screw and we had to push-mow the yard for a month. Man, my dad was furious. But, uh... sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, emotions. Yeah, no, I think I'm feeling things normally. Nothing's really changed there.
Have you noticed a decrease in how much you enjoy the things you usually like to do?

Enjoy things? Hmm, no, I'd say I still enjoy my usual stuff just as much. Like, I still go bowling on Thursday nights with a couple of the guys from the station. We're in this casual league, nothing too serious. Though my buddy Dave takes it way too seriously. He just bought this custom bowling ball online, cost him like two hundred bucks. It's got this crazy swirl pattern, looks almost like a bowling ball version of Jupiter, you know? With the big red spot and everything. Speaking of Jupiter, my youngest had to do a science fair project on the solar system last week. We spent three hours painting these little styrofoam balls. The paint got absolutely everywhere. Turns out acrylic paint does not come out of a kitchen rug very easily. We tried club soda, vinegar, even that foaming carpet cleaner you see on the infomercials late at night. You know the one, with the guy with the really loud voice who always yelled about the power of oxygen or whatever? I bought a mop from one of those commercials once. The handle snapped the second time I used it to clean the kitchen floor. Total piece of junk. I ended up using the broken handle as a stake for my pepper plants, so I guess it wasn't a complete waste of money. Gardening is all about improvising anyway, you just kind of use what you have lying around. But... hang on, what was the question? Enjoying things? Right. Yeah, no, I haven't noticed any decrease. I'm still having fun doing my normal stuff.
Do you think your father-in-law moving in is the main reason you're feeling this way?

Yeah, I definitely think so. I mean, I came in because ever since he moved in with us, I've just been... well, I hold it together at work, but at home and with my coursework, I'm way more wound up and short-tempered than I'm used to being. And I've even started skipping out on things that usually keep my head clear, like fishing, my woodworking projects, and those first-aid workshops I usually help out with. Woodworking used to be my big escape, you know? I was building this beautiful cedar chest for my wife. Cedar smells incredible when you cut it. Reminds me of this cabin my uncle used to rent up in Maine when I was a teenager. We'd go up there every August, and the whole place just smelled like pine needles and old campfire smoke. My uncle had this ancient Ford pickup truck, cherry red, with a manual transmission. He taught me how to drive stick in that thing on these old logging roads. I stalled it about fifty times the first day. The clutch was so stiff you practically had to stand on it to get it to engage. I drove a stick shift for years after that. Had a little Honda Civic in my twenties, great gas mileage. I could fill the tank for like, twenty bucks back then. Gas prices now are just out of control. I saw a station yesterday charging almost four dollars a gallon. It's ridiculous. Makes you want to buy an electric car, but then you have to worry about finding charging stations, and I heard the batteries cost a fortune to replace if they go bad. My neighbor bought an electric lawnmower last summer, and he loves it. It's so quiet, you barely even know he's mowing. Not like my gas mower, which sounds like a jet engine taking off. I really need to change the spark plug on that thing before spring. But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my father-in-law. Yeah, it's definitely him moving in that's got me feeling this way, skipping my hobbies and just being so on edge at home.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy doing?

Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I still really like all the stuff I usually do, I just haven't been doing it as much, like I said. But the interest is definitely still there. Like with fishing, I was actually just looking at a new tackle box online yesterday. My old one has a cracked hinge from when I dropped it in the driveway last summer. It landed right on the concrete and all my hooks spilled everywhere. Took me an hour to pick them up, and I was terrified my dog was going to step on one. He's a golden retriever, total goofball, always getting into things. Last week he managed to open the pantry door and ate half a loaf of bread. The plastic bag and everything. We had to take him to the emergency vet at two in the morning. 

The vet there was this young kid, looked barely out of high school. It's crazy how young doctors and vets look to me now. Makes me feel old, you know? I'm fifty-one and my knees definitely remind me of it every time I climb into the back of the ambulance. We have these new power stretchers at work that are supposed to save your back, but they're honestly heavier to maneuver than the old manual ones. The sales rep who sold them to the department came in to do a training session, and he was wearing this suit that was just way too tight. You could tell he was sweating bullets the whole time he was demonstrating the lifting mechanism. He kept tugging at his collar. I almost offered him a bottle of water, but he packed up and left so fast. 

But, uh... sorry, I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? Losing interest? Right. No, the interest is still there. I still want to do my hobbies, I just haven't been as active with them lately.
Do you feel like you're really connecting with your family and friends emotionally like you used to?

Connecting? Yeah, I'd say I'm still connecting with everyone just fine. I mean, my wife and I still talk every night, and I'm still keeping up with the guys from the station. Like I said, we've got the bowling league, and there's this group chat we have going. It's mostly just memes and complaining about dispatch, honestly. Dispatch has been a nightmare lately. They got this new computer-aided dispatch system, CAD they call it, and it's supposed to streamline everything, but it just crashes all the time. Last Tuesday we were sitting in the rig for twenty minutes waiting for an address to load. We ended up having to use the radio like it was 1995. 

I remember back when I first started as an EMT, we didn't have any of this fancy GPS stuff. You had to know the streets, or you had a massive map book in the cab. You'd be flying down the road with the sirens on, flipping through this giant binder trying to find some obscure cul-de-sac. It was wild. My first partner was this guy named Stan, old-school guy, smoked a pack a day, even in the ambulance sometimes if we were parked. You could never get away with that now. Stan knew every pothole in the city. He retired and moved to Florida, bought a condo right on the beach. He sends me pictures sometimes of him just sitting there with a margarita. I went to Florida once for a conference, Orlando I think. The humidity was unbelievable. You walk outside and it's like wearing a wet blanket. We went to one of those theme parks on our day off and I paid twelve dollars for a hot dog. Twelve dollars! And it didn't even come with fries. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Connecting with people? Right, yeah. No, I haven't noticed any issues there. Still feel just as close to my family and friends as always.
Have you found it difficult to perform your job as an EMT or complete your coursework since your father-in-law moved in?

Well, work is... I'm still doing my EMT shifts, getting through them okay, but the coursework is another story. I'm trying to get my paramedic certification, and I've definitely fallen behind on the reading and assignments since he got here. And those community first-aid workshops I mentioned earlier? I used to help out with those almost every weekend, but I haven't been showing up consistently for those either. 

It's a shame, too, because I really like teaching those workshops. We get a lot of new parents coming in, wanting to know infant CPR and what to do if their kid chokes on a grape. Grapes are so dangerous for toddlers, you know? You really have to cut them into quarters, not just in half. My wife used to be so paranoid about that when our kids were little. She had this special little gadget that would slice the grapes perfectly. We bought it at one of those kitchen supply stores in the mall. You know, the ones that sell like, a specific tool for coring an apple, and another one just for peeling garlic? I don't know how those stores stay in business. Who needs a strawberry huller? Just use a knife! We had a knife block on our counter for years, but then I read somewhere that those blocks are basically breeding grounds for bacteria because you can't ever clean inside the slots. So I threw it out and got one of those magnetic strips that goes on the wall. It looks pretty cool, very professional, like a restaurant kitchen. 

I worked in a restaurant kitchen for a summer when I was in college. Worst job I ever had. It was a seafood place, and my hands smelled like shrimp for three months straight. I couldn't even eat shrimp for years after that. My buddy Dave, he loves shrimp. He can eat his weight in that shrimp cocktail stuff they have at weddings. Dave's the guy I bowl with on Thursdays. He just got a new bowling ball, custom drilled and everything. It's got this crazy swirl pattern on it, looks like a bowling ball from the future. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, right, work and school. Yeah, EMT work is fine, just behind on the paramedic classes and skipping the first-aid workshops.
Have you felt like your relationships with family and friends have been affected by how you've been feeling since your father-in-law moved in?

Affected? No, I wouldn't say that. Like I said before, I'm still talking to my wife every night, still hanging out with the guys from the station. Everything's pretty much the same there. My father-in-law being here hasn't really changed how I get along with people. He mostly just watches TV anyway. He loves those old Westerns, you know? The ones in black and white where the good guy always wears a white hat. 

I actually tried watching one with him the other day. It was... well, it was slow. Not like the movies they make now. We went to see that new action movie a few weeks ago, the one with the car chases? Unbelievable special effects. The theater we went to had those reclining seats, the leather ones that go all the way back. You could practically fall asleep in them. Honestly, I almost did. I was coming off a night shift and I was exhausted. Night shifts are brutal when you hit your fifties. Your body just doesn't bounce back the same way. I used to be able to work a twelve-hour night shift, grab a coffee, and go straight to a baseball game. 

I used to love going to baseball games. The smell of the grass, the crack of the bat. My dad used to take me when I was a kid. We'd always get seats way up in the nosebleeds, but we didn't care. We'd bring our own peanuts in a paper bag. You can't even do that anymore, they check your bags at the gate now. Security is so tight everywhere. Even at the hospital, you have to badge in through like three different doors just to get to the breakroom. And the breakroom coffee is terrible. It tastes like it's been sitting on the burner since Tuesday. 

But, um... sorry, what were you asking? Relationships? Yeah, no, my relationships are fine. No problems there.
Have you felt like your father-in-law moving in has significantly impacted your ability to function at work or at home?

Well, like I was telling you a minute ago, my actual EMT shifts are fine. I'm getting through work okay. But it's the other stuff that's slipping—I've definitely fallen behind on my paramedic coursework, and I stopped showing up consistently for those community first-aid workshops I usually help out with. At home, it's just harder to focus on things like studying. I actually went to the public library last week just to get some peace and quiet to read my textbook.

I haven't been to that library in years, honestly. They completely renovated the inside since the last time I was there. It looks like a spaceship now, all glass and brushed metal everywhere. I tried to check out a supplemental book on cardiac life support, but the librarian told me I had a late fee from like, 2018. It was for this paperback thriller my wife wanted me to read. She loves those mystery books, the ones where you don't know who the killer is until the very last page. She buys them by the dozen at those weekend thrift sales. We have these huge wooden bookshelves in the hallway just overflowing with them. 

I keep telling her we should just get one of those e-readers, you know? Save some space. My buddy Dave has one, and he takes it out on his boat when he goes fishing. He caught a massive bass last weekend, actually. Sent a picture to our group chat. He's always trying to get me to go out on the water with him, but I get terrible seasickness. Even just on a lake, if the water gets a little choppy, my stomach just does backflips. I tried those little wristbands they sell at the pharmacy, the ones that press on your pressure points? Didn't do a thing for me. Total waste of fourteen bucks. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, how I'm functioning. Yeah, like I said, mostly it's just the paramedic classes and skipping those first-aid workshops. Everything else is mostly okay.
Have you felt like your current state is significantly interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Well, like I think I just mentioned a minute ago, my relationships are totally fine, but as far as my daily life goes... I'm still doing my regular EMT shifts without any problems. It's just the extra stuff. I've fallen behind on some of my paramedic coursework, and I stopped showing up consistently for the community first-aid workshops I usually help with. 

Those workshops are held at the rec center downtown, and honestly, finding parking there is a nightmare anyway. They have these huge pine trees around the lot that drop sap all over your windshield. I parked under one last fall and had to use half a bottle of rubbing alcohol just to get the sticky spots off my truck. My neighbor, Gary, swore by using peanut butter to remove tree sap. Can you believe that? Peanut butter. I told him he was crazy, but he brought over a jar of chunky Jif and just smeared it right on his hood. The neighborhood dogs wouldn't leave his car alone for a week! 

Gary's a good guy, though. He always snowblows my driveway when it gets really bad out. We had a blizzard a couple years ago that dumped three feet in one night, and the city plows didn't come through our street for two days. We just sat inside drinking hot cocoa and watching the local news. I always laugh when the news channels make their reporters stand out on the highway in the middle of a snowstorm, looking absolutely miserable. Why do they do that? We know it's snowing! We don't need a guy in a parka getting blown over by the wind to prove it. I mean, it's just a ratings grab, right? 

But, uh... sorry, I lost my train of thought. What were we just talking about? Oh, interfering with my life. Right. Yeah, so just falling behind on the paramedic classes and skipping the workshops, really. My actual EMT job is fine.
Do you feel like your current situation is causing you a lot of distress or significantly impacting your ability to function?

Well, I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, Doc. Like I said, I'm still doing my regular EMT shifts, that's going fine. It's really just that I've fallen behind on my paramedic coursework, and I haven't been going to those community first-aid workshops I usually help out with. 

I used to really enjoy those workshops, actually. We'd set up in the gymnasium at the community center, and they always had these big folding tables that were impossible to lock into place. One time, someone leaned too hard on one of the tables while practicing chest compressions on a dummy, and the whole thing just collapsed. The dummy went flying across the floor, and this poor lady who was trying to learn CPR looked absolutely horrified. It was funny, though. We all had a good laugh. 

Laughter is important, you know? Especially in my line of work. You see a lot of heavy stuff, so you have to find the humor where you can. My partner on the rig, Sarah, she's great at that. She has this whole collection of terrible dad jokes that she pulls out whenever we're stuck in traffic on the way back to the station. The other day she asked me, "Why don't skeletons fight each other?" And I said I didn't know, and she goes, "They don't have the guts!" I mean, it's terrible, right? But you can't help but chuckle. She buys these little joke books from the dollar store near the hospital. 

That dollar store is actually pretty amazing. They have everything in there. I went in to buy a birthday card for my niece last month and ended up walking out with three bags of gardening soil and a plastic flamingo. I don't even have a garden! I just thought the flamingo was funny. I stuck it right in the middle of my front lawn. My wife hates it, but I think it gives the yard character. 

Anyway... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, distress and functioning. Yeah, so just the coursework and the workshops, really. I'm getting by otherwise.
Do you feel like you're experiencing significant anxiety most of the time?

Anxiety? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel nervous or panicked all day or anything like that. I guess the only time I really feel jittery is if I drink way too much coffee. 

There's this new place that just opened up right down the street from the station, called The Daily Grind or something clever like that. They serve this cold brew that is absolute rocket fuel. I had a large one last Tuesday and I swear my heart was beating out of my chest for four hours. The guy who works there, the barista, he's got these crazy full-sleeve tattoos. Really intricate stuff, like dragons and koi fish and all these colorful waves. Must have cost him an absolute fortune. 

I watch those tattoo competition shows on TV sometimes with my wife, you know the ones? Where they have like, three hours to do a photorealistic portrait and the judges are always yelling about their line work and shading. I don't know how they do it under that kind of pressure. If someone was grading my EMT charting on live television, I'd probably freeze up completely. Though, to be fair, my handwriting is pretty terrible anyway. Doctors always get a bad rap for messy handwriting, but let me tell you, medics are just as bad. We write half our patient reports bouncing around in the back of a moving ambulance, hitting every single pothole in the city. The city really needs to fix the roads on the east side, honestly. It's getting ridiculous. I hit a crater on Elm Street last month that I thought for sure was going to blow out my front tire. 

But, uh... wait, hang on. You were asking about anxiety, right? Yeah, sorry. No, I don't really feel anxious most of the time. Just normal stuff, really. No constant anxiety.

doctor.intent: determine presence of avoidant behavior

We had a blizzard a couple years ago that dumped three feet in one night, and the city plows didn't come through our street for two days. We just sat inside drinking hot cocoa and watching the local news. I always laugh when the news channels make their reporters stand out on the highway in the middle of a snowstorm, looking absolutely miserable. Why do they do that? We know it's snowing! We don't need a guy in a parka getting blown over by the wind to prove it. I mean, it's just a ratings grab, right? 

But, uh... sorry, I lost my train of thought. What were we just talking about? Oh, interfering with my life. Right. Yeah, so just falling behind on the paramedic classes and skipping the workshops, really. My actual EMT job is fine.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment
doctor.question: Do you feel like your current situation is causing you a lot of distress or significantly impacting your ability to function?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still doing my EMT work, but I’ve fallen behind on some paramedic coursework and stopped showing up consistently for the community first-aid workshops I usually help with.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about distress or significant impact on the ability to function, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, Doc. Like I said, I'm still doing my regular EMT shifts, that's going fine. It's really just that I've fallen behind on my paramedic coursework, and I haven't been going to those community first-aid workshops I usually help out with. 

I used to really enjoy those workshops, actually. We'd set up in the gymnasium at the community center, and they always had these big folding tables that were impossible to lock into place. One time, someone leaned too hard on one of the tables while practicing chest compressions on a dummy, and the whole thing just collapsed. The dummy went flying across the floor, and this poor lady who was trying to learn CPR looked absolutely horrified. It was funny, though. We all had a good laugh. 

Laughter is important, you know? Especially in my line of work. You see a lot of heavy stuff, so you have to find the humor where you can. My partner on the rig, Sarah, she's great at that. She has this whole collection of terrible dad jokes that she pulls out whenever we're stuck in traffic on the way back to the station. The other day she asked me, "Why don't skeletons fight each other?" And I said I didn't know, and she goes, "They don't have the guts!" I mean, it's terrible, right? But you can't help but chuckle. She buys these little joke books from the dollar store near the hospital. 

That dollar store is actually pretty amazing. They have everything in there. I went in to buy a birthday card for my niece last month and ended up walking out with three bags of gardening soil and a plastic flamingo. I don't even have a garden! I just thought the flamingo was funny. I stuck it right in the middle of my front lawn. My wife hates it, but I think it gives the yard character. 

Anyway... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, distress and functioning. Yeah, so just the coursework and the workshops, really. I'm getting by otherwise.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant anxiety
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're experiencing significant anxiety most of the time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant anxiety most of the time, which is a symptom of Generalized Anxiety Disorder or other anxiety disorders. My symptom profile only contains items related to Adjustment Disorder and does not have a specific item for general anxiety.

patient.answer:
Anxiety? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel nervous or panicked all day or anything like that. I guess the only time I really feel jittery is if I drink way too much coffee. 

There's this new place that just opened up right down the street from the station, called The Daily Grind or something clever like that. They serve this cold brew that is absolute rocket fuel. I had a large one last Tuesday and I swear my heart was beating out of my chest for four hours. The guy who works there, the barista, he's got these crazy full-sleeve tattoos. Really intricate stuff, like dragons and koi fish and all these colorful waves. Must have cost him an absolute fortune. 

I watch those tattoo competition shows on TV sometimes with my wife, you know the ones? Where they have like, three hours to do a photorealistic portrait and the judges are always yelling about their line work and shading. I don't know how they do it under that kind of pressure. If someone was grading my EMT charting on live television, I'd probably freeze up completely. Though, to be fair, my handwriting is pretty terrible anyway. Doctors always get a bad rap for messy handwriting, but let me tell you, medics are just as bad. We write half our patient reports bouncing around in the back of a moving ambulance, hitting every single pothole in the city. The city really needs to fix the roads on the east side, honestly. It's getting ridiculous. I hit a crater on Elm Street last month that I thought for sure was going to blow out my front tire. 

But, uh... wait, hang on. You were asking about anxiety, right? Yeah, sorry. No, I don't really feel anxious most of the time. Just normal stuff, really. No constant anxiety.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of increased irritability, being 'wound up,' and having no patience, especially since his father-in-law moved in, align more closely with an adjustment disorder with irritability, given the absence of pervasive sadness, anxiety, or loss of interest in activities.
